subject: math
title: Grade 1 Concrete Graphs: Sort, Count and Compare
seo_title: Grade 1 Concrete Graphs Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Grade 1 math worksheets on concrete graphs for the BC curriculum: sort and count real things, read graphs of fruit and cube towers where 1 object = 1, find the most and the fewest, and answer how many more questions about class data. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: In a concrete graph, 1 thing = 1. Start every row at the same line, then count.
key_sub: Sort first, then count one group. Touch each thing once. The longest row or tallest tower has the most. How many more means match one to one and count what is left over.
body_html:
The big idea

A concrete graph is a graph made of real things. It can use fruit, toys, shoes or connecting cubes. One thing stands for one. This is called one-to-one correspondence.

Sort, then count

First, sort the things into groups. Then count each group. Touch each thing once as you count.

Make and read the graph

Put each group in its own row. Every row starts at the same line. Put one thing in each square. Then the longest row has the most.

We can also use cube towers. Each student puts one cube on a tower. The tallest tower has the most.

Count, do not just look

If things are spread out, a row can look long. Match the things one to one, or count them.

How many more?

How many more and how many fewer mean compare. Match the rows one to one. Count the ones left over. Altogether means add.

How many more?

Apple 6, Pear 4. How many more votes did Apple get than Pear?

Match 4 apples with 4 pears. 2 apples are left over. 6 − 4 = 2.

Answer: 2 more votes

How many altogether?

Apple 6, Banana 3, Pear 4. How many votes were there altogether?

6 + 3 + 4 = 13.

Answer: 13 votes

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting all the things, not one groupSort first, then count only that group
Counting a thing twice or skipping oneTouch each thing once as you count
Reading the row above or belowPut your finger on the label, then read that row
Picking the row that looks longestCount, or match one to one
Adding when it asks how many moreHow many more means compare: find what is left over

faq.q: What is a concrete graph in Grade 1 math?
faq.a: A concrete graph is made of real things, such as fruit, shoes or connecting cubes, lined up in rows or towers. Each thing stands for one, so students can count and compare the rows.

faq.q: What does one-to-one correspondence mean on a graph?
faq.a: It means one object stands for one piece of data, such as one cube for each student’s vote. Matching two rows one to one shows which row has more and how many more.

faq.q: What do Grade 1 students learn about data in the BC math curriculum?
faq.a: In the BC Grade 1 Data and probability area, students make and read concrete graphs using one-to-one correspondence. They sort, count, compare which has more or fewer, and talk about what the graph shows.

faq.q: How can I practise concrete graphs with my Grade 1 child at home?
faq.a: Sort snacks, socks or toy cars into rows that start at the same line. Ask which row has the most, which has the fewest and how many more one row has than another.
